title: MSE vs MAE
interviewAnswer: Use MSE when you want large errors penalized disproportionately because errors are squared. Use MAE when you want a loss that grows linearly and is more robust to outliers. The choice is about error behavior—not whether the current loss value is “large” or “small.”
why: This is a classic interview question because it tests whether you understand how a loss function changes model behavior, not whether you can recite formulas.
intuition: Imagine residuals [1, 1, 1, 10]. MAE treats the large error as 10; MSE turns it into 100. That single point therefore dominates MSE much more strongly.
deepDive: MSE is smooth everywhere and its gradient grows with error magnitude, so large residuals drive larger updates. MAE has a constant-magnitude gradient away from zero and is more robust to extreme residuals. Statistically, minimizing expected squared error targets the conditional mean, while minimizing expected absolute error targets the conditional median.
code:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([0., 0., 0., 0.])
y_hat = np.array([1., 1., 1., 10.])
errors = y - y_hat
print('MAE:', np.mean(np.abs(errors)))
print('MSE:', np.mean(errors ** 2))
commonMistakes: “Use MSE when the loss is big and MAE when it is small.” — incorrect. The choice is about error weighting and assumptions.
“MAE ignores large errors.” — false; it penalizes them linearly rather than quadratically.
Comparing raw MSE and MAE magnitudes as if they were on the same units; MSE is in squared target units.
followUps: How does Huber loss combine MAE and MSE behavior?

production: Choose the metric/loss from business error cost. A model may train with one differentiable loss and still be selected using a different operational metric.
workedExample: If one price prediction is off by €100 while most are off by €5, MSE strongly prioritizes fixing the €100 miss. MAE is less dominated by that single outlier.

lab.goal: Make outlier sensitivity visible rather than memorizing definitions.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
y=np.array([10,10,10,10.])
p1=np.array([9,11,10,30.])
err=p1-y
mae=np.mean(np.abs(err)); mse=np.mean(err**2)
print('errors',err,'MAE',mae,'MSE',mse)

visual.title: How error size changes the penalty
visual.caption: MAE grows linearly with residual magnitude; MSE grows quadratically, so large errors receive much more weight.
